package_info.package_manager: malware (multi-stage, distributed via phishing, not a public package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple variants (including .NET and Rust-based backdoors), active as of March 2023
package_info.why_malicious: Mispandu is a banking trojan distributed through phishing campaigns, specifically designed to steal credentials from banking, email, and social media services. It uses obfuscated payloads, fake certificates, and multiple backdoor components. The malware leverages compromised infrastructure for command and control (C2), automates payload delivery, establishes persistence, and exfiltrates sensitive data to attacker-controlled servers. Its multi-stage architecture and use of misleading filenames and locations make it highly evasive and dangerous.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Factura_Deuda_423534.cmd (batch script, content not shown, but launches next-stage payloads)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the phishing attachment, the CMD script executes, downloads additional payloads from attacker-controlled URLs, writes them to disk, and launches them, resulting in malware installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: CMD scripts disguised as invoices are a well-known malware delivery method, especially when delivered via phishing emails.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate invoices should be non-executable documents (e.g., PDF, XLSX), not scripts capable of launching further code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated IT maintenance scripts, but never distributed as invoices or bills to end users.
key_indicators: Located in AppData with randomized subfolders
Initiates download and execution of further payloads

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: sastreria.xls.exe (PE executable, content not shown, likely initial dropper or loader)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user double-clicks the file, the executable runs, downloads or unpacks the main trojan payload, writes it to disk, and establishes persistence mechanisms.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a double file extension (.xls.exe) is a classic technique to trick users into executing malware, as it appears to be a document.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Excel files should not be executable binaries and should not have double extensions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; double extensions are almost exclusively used for malicious purposes.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At system startup, the shortcut automatically launches the main trojan executable from a non-standard location, ensuring the malware persists across reboots.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly abuses the Startup folder to maintain persistence, especially with misleading shortcut names.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate audio drivers do not create userland startup shortcuts with misleading names or point to executables in random AppData subfolders.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software uses startup shortcuts, but typically with clear naming and standard installation paths.
key_indicators: Suspiciously named shortcut in Startup folder
Shortcut points to executable in non-standard AppData path
Used in conjunction with other malware indicators

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: jordan.exe (main trojan, .NET or Rust-based, capable of screenshots, credential theft, fake windows, C2 communication)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the trojan executes, accesses browser and email credential stores, captures screenshots, and sends harvested data to C2 servers via HTTP(S) POST requests, resulting in credential exfiltration and remote attacker control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The combination of credential theft, screenshotting, and C2 communication is characteristic of banking trojans targeting sensitive user data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not access or exfiltrate credentials, take screenshots, or communicate with known malicious infrastructure without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support tools may access similar resources, but only with explicit user awareness and consent.
key_indicators: Access to credential stores and screenshot APIs
Outbound HTTP(S) POST requests to known C2 domains/IPs
Executable located in non-standard AppData subfolder

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: gnVzjGd.vbs (VBScript, likely used to launch or stage other payloads)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When executed, the VBScript launches or downloads additional payloads, or acts as a loader for the main trojan, enabling further stages of the attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Randomly named VBS files in public directories are a common technique for malware staging and lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts are not randomly named or placed in public folders accessible to all users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare; legitimate scripts are usually named descriptively and stored in predictable locations.
key_indicators: Script launches or downloads further payloads
Used as a loader or stager for main trojan

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with HTML or password-protected PDF attachment masquerading as an invoice or bill.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens attachment, triggering initial payload

attack_chain.action: User executes disguised script or executable (e.g., .cmd or .xls.exe), which downloads and runs additional malware components.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware establishes persistence and launches main trojan

attack_chain.action: Malware creates persistence mechanism via startup shortcut in the Startup folder, pointing to the main trojan executable.
attack_chain.leads_to: Trojan runs at every system startup

attack_chain.action: Main trojan (jordan.exe) executes, harvesting credentials, taking screenshots, and communicating with C2 servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive data to attacker

attack_chain.action: Staging scripts (e.g., gnVzjGd.vbs) may be used to launch or update payloads, supporting sustained infection and further payload delivery.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sustained infection and possible further payload delivery

behavioral_signatures: Execution of scripts or executables with double extensions (e.g., .xls.exe) from user Downloads folder
Creation of startup shortcuts in the Startup folder pointing to executables in non-standard AppData subfolders
Processes accessing browser, email, or system credential stores and invoking screenshot APIs
Outbound HTTP(S) POST requests to known C2 domains/IPs following suspicious process activity
Presence and execution of randomly named VBS scripts in %PUBLIC% directory
network_indicators: Multiple URLs with /do/it.php, /img/, /rest/?h=CODE, etc. (see IOCs above)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of files with double extensions (e.g., .xls.exe) in user directories, creation of suspicious startup shortcuts in the Startup folder pointing to executables in AppData, and processes accessing credential stores or invoking screenshot APIs. Correlate these behaviors with outbound connections to known C2 domains/IPs and the presence of files matching known IOCs in AppData, Startup, and Public folders. Use endpoint detection to flag .NET or Rust executables with credential access and screenshot capabilities, especially if communicating with listed C2 infrastructure. Alert on the presence and execution of randomly named VBS scripts in %PUBLIC% directory.
